context: linear in live streets · utility diversions first, then track slab, overhead line, systems and trial running

brief.intro: New to this project type? A tram or light-rail line is a railway built in the middle of a working city street. Before any track can be laid, every pipe and cable under the future track must be moved out of the way — utility diversion is usually the longest and least predictable part of the job. Then the street is rebuilt in stages, keeping traffic moving: track slab and embedded rails, stops, the overhead contact line and its traction substations, signalling and priority at road junctions, and the depot where the trams are stabled and maintained. The trams themselves are ordered years ahead. The last months are testing: each system alone, then all together, then trial running without passengers, before the safety authority allows opening.

glossary.plain: relocating buried services so they are not under the track and can be maintained without closing the line.
the rail used in streets, with a groove for the wheel flange so road vehicles can cross it.
rail encapsulated in the road surface, with elastic material that reduces noise and stray current.
the overhead wire the tram takes its power from.
the substation that converts grid power to the DC voltage of the tram line.
current leaking from the rails into the ground, which corrodes buried pipes; the track is insulated to prevent it.
traffic signals that give the tram a green as it approaches.
running trams to the full timetable without passengers to prove the system and train the staff.
testing the line with a tram actually moving on it.

must_get_right: Put the utility diversions at the front of the schedule with realistic durations and each utility owner's approvals — track work cannot start in a street section until they are finished.
Plan by street section and traffic stage: the city authority limits how many sections can be closed at once, and that limit is the real resource.
Rolling stock, traction substations and signalling are long-lead; the first tram must arrive in time for dynamic testing, and the depot must be ready to receive it.
Reserve several months for system integration tests, trial running and the safety authority's approval — they cannot be compressed at the end.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities are organised by street section and traffic stage for civil and track, and by system for the line-wide works, with the depot and rolling stock as separate branches.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Standard site calendar with city restrictions (events, holidays, night work near homes). Junction closures are weekend or night possessions.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: Per section: approvals → utility diversions → track bed and slab → rails → embedding → road reinstatement. Line-wide: substations and OCS → energisation → signalling and telecom → system tests. Depot ready → first tram delivered → dynamic tests → integration → trial running → approval. The critical path usually runs through utility diversions in the hardest section, or through rolling stock.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Utility owners approve and attend diversions in the assumed time; the traffic authority grants the planned stages; the grid connection for traction substations is available; rolling stock is delivered to the contract dates.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: The schedule tracks the following as milestones because they drive the programme:

rows: Before track laying in the first section

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: A live city: limited road closures, access for residents and shops, noise limits, archaeology in old centres.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Main risks: unknown or badly recorded utilities, traffic-stage refusals, late rolling stock, integration problems between systems, and conditions set by the safety authority. Contingency is held before the start of trial running.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 by street section and system; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the diversion, track and systems crews — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
